terrain.difficultyNotes: A three-tier breakdown, so percentExpert is null and the top 27% sits in percentAdvanced. These are the resort's own figures, read from attitash.com's mountain information page after Vail's web estate came back up; the file previously carried OnTheSnow's 22/49/29 split, which moved 7 points from the beginner grade into intermediate and overstated how much of the mountain is middle-grade skiing. Attitash is really two mountains - Attitash proper and Bear Peak, linked mid-mountain - and the 76-trail count covers both. The resort also publishes 60+ acres of tree skiing and 23 miles of trails, which is the more useful way to think about a mountain whose acreage figure is modest. The one figure still worth treating carefully is snowfall: see dataDisputes.

passes.name: Epic Local Pass
passes.access: Unlimited - Attitash is on the Epic Local unlimited list alongside Crotched Mountain, Mount Snow, Mount Sunapee, Okemo and Wildcat

pricing.notes: 2026-27 season. Vail prices day tickets dynamically by date and publishes no fixed window rate, so the ticket fields are null rather than estimated. The season pass figure is the full adult (31+) Epic Pass; Vail does not sell an unrestricted Attitash-only pass. Attitash carries unlimited access on the cheaper Epic Local Pass too, at $829 for 31+, which is the tier most New England Epic buyers actually want. Every content page on attitash.com became readable again on 2026-08-25 and this file was rebuilt from them, but the ticket and pass pages are a separate matter: they redirect to Vail's ecommerce waiting room, which requires JavaScript, so no pass or ticket price on any Vail property could be read from the operator directly. The $1,119 therefore still comes from OnTheSnow's Epic buyer's guide - specifically its current-cost line, not its prose, which quotes the March 2026 on-sale price of $1,089.

editorial.overview: Attitash is the mountain the Mount Washington Valley actually skis, and it is a more interesting place than its statistics suggest. Seventeen hundred and fifty feet of vertical across two linked peaks - Attitash proper and Bear Peak - on 311 acres in Bartlett, ten minutes from North Conway and all the lodging, food and outlet shopping the valley has. That location is the whole proposition: Attitash is where a family staying in North Conway goes, and it sits at the unlimited tier on both the full Epic Pass and the Epic Local, which makes it close to free for anyone who already holds one. The skiing is honest terrain with a long runout, a three-mile top-to-bottom and 76 trails split 29/44/27, with 60-odd acres of tree skiing threaded through it. The problem is elevation. The base sits at 600 feet - the lowest on this roster - and the summit at 2,350, so what falls on Wildcat as snow arrives here as rain more often than anyone would like, and the lower third of the hill takes the worst of every thaw. Attitash lives or dies on snowmaking and on the calendar. In a cold February it is a genuinely good mountain and the Bear Peak side gives it more variety than the acreage implies. In a mild one it is the thinnest big-name mountain in New Hampshire.
editorial.snowQuality: The weak point, and the sources disagree about how weak. Attitash publishes a 120-inch average; OnTheSnow records 88. Take either and it is a low total for northern New Hampshire, and the reason is elevation rather than latitude: a 600-foot base on the Mount Washington Valley floor catches a great deal of rain in storms that fall as snow on the surrounding mountains, and Wildcat is twenty minutes up the road and two thousand feet higher with roughly double the natural snow. Snowmaking covers 240 of the 311 acres by OnTheSnow's count and it is doing the heavy lifting all season rather than just at the margins. This is a mountain to ski in a cold spell, and one where reading the base-area report matters more than at almost anywhere else on this roster.
editorial.crowds: Busier than it looks on paper, because Attitash draws from a large lodging base rather than from day-trippers. North Conway fills up over school holidays and February vacation, and the valley's visitors distribute themselves between Attitash, Cranmore and Wildcat - with Attitash taking the largest share of the families. Eight lifts across two linked peaks spreads people reasonably well, and Bear Peak stays quieter than the Attitash side. The pattern worth knowing is that Epic Pass access at the unlimited tier makes this a default choice for a lot of New England passholders, so weekends draw a passholder crowd on top of the resort's own guests.
editorial.difficulty: Comfortable rather than testing. The resort's own three-tier split puts 44% in the middle grade and 27% at the top, which is an accurate description - this is a mountain of long, well-cut intermediate trails with a three-mile top-to-bottom run and enough pitch on the upper sections to keep a competent skier interested. The two-peak layout adds variety the acreage does not suggest, and there are 60-plus acres of tree skiing; Attitash's own guidance sends experts to the narrow, classic New England lines of Tim's and Ptarmigan off the Mountaineer quad, and intermediates across to Bear Peak's wide groomers. What is missing is anything sustained or steep enough to worry a genuine expert, and the low base means the bottom third is often the least pleasant part of the run rather than the payoff. Anyone in the valley looking for real difficulty drives to Wildcat.

keyTrails.name: Tim's Trail
keyTrails.note: Narrow, classic New England skiing off the Mountaineer quad - the resort's own answer to where experts should go, and the opposite in character to Bear Peak.

keyTrails.name: Ptarmigan
keyTrails.note: The other half of that answer: tight, old-school and served by the Mountaineer. The name also survives on Ptarmigans Pub in the base lodge and the pop-up park out front.

keyTrails.name: Illusion
keyTrails.note: Bear Peak's race trail, which Attitash calls one of the region's most sought-after alpine race courses. Steep, wide and consistently pitched.

keyTrails.name: Bear Peak
keyTrails.note: The second mountain, linked mid-mountain and consistently quieter than the Attitash side. Wide open groomers and glades, added in the mid-1990s.

keyTrails.name: The Mountaineer
keyTrails.note: The summit quad on the Attitash side, and the lift that defines a day here - it serves the longest sustained descents on the hill.

tidbits: Attitash is two linked mountains - Attitash proper and Bear Peak - counted as one resort.
It opened in 1965 as the Red Carpet Ski Area, known for capping day-ticket sales to keep lift lines short.
The 600-foot base elevation is the lowest of any mountain in this guide.
Bear Peak was added in the mid-1990s and is still the quieter half.
The resort claims 120 inches of snow a year; OnTheSnow records 88.
Attitash publishes 60+ acres of tree skiing and 23 miles of trails.
Attitash is unlimited on the Epic Local Pass as well as the full Epic Pass.
Published lift hours never run past 4pm, so there is no night skiing - unlike its sister mountain Crotched.

dataDisputes.note: A 32-inch gap. The resort's own mountain information page publishes a 120-inch average; OnTheSnow records 88. The resort's figure is stored because CLAUDE.md prefers the resort's own site, but the lower number is the one to plan a natural-snow trip around, and it is worth knowing that neither figure is generous by New England standards - Attitash's 600-foot base is the lowest on this roster and takes rain in storms that fall as snow on the mountains around it.

moguls.policy: No grooming policy is published. Attitash's own site, readable again as of this revision, describes its terrain and its parks in detail and says nothing about which trails are left ungroomed, and no independent review consulted names a bump run here. What is recorded is inference from terrain and snow rather than anything stated.
moguls.quality: Not documented, and this file says so rather than filling the gap. What can be said from the sourced figures is structural: a low base, a snowfall average somewhere between 88 and 120 inches and snowmaking over 240 of 311 acres mean Attitash depends on machine snow for most of its surface, and a heavily snowmade surface gets groomed to stay usable. That points to a mountain where bumps form between passes on the narrow upper pitches - Tim's and Ptarmigan are the candidates - rather than one with maintained mogul terrain. Anyone in the Mount Washington Valley specifically wanting bumps should drive to Wildcat, which does not groom its blacks at all.

parks.name: Arcade Park
parks.note: The main park and the one the freestyle crowd comes for: unique rail and box features, small and medium jumps, and large jumps. No feature counts are published.

parks.name: Ptarmigans Pop Up Park
parks.note: Smaller features set up in front of the Main Base Lodge, and explicitly weather and conditions permitting - so it is there some days and not others.

parks.name: Family Cross
parks.note: A skier-cross style course rather than a jib park - rollers and turns aimed at families. Counted in the resort's park total.

parks.progression: A clean three-step ladder, and unusually explicit about where the bottom rung is: Ptarmigans Pop Up in front of the base lodge for first features, Family Cross for anyone who wants terrain rather than jibs, and Arcade Park for the real thing. The gap is in the middle - Arcade carries small through large jumps in one park rather than splitting them, so the step from the pop-up park into Arcade is bigger than the three-park count suggests.
parks.overview: Three parks, collectively branded Arcade Terrain Parks, and the resort's own count and description agree - 3 in the mountain statistics block and three named parks on the terrain parks page. Arcade Park is the main event, with rail and box features and jumps up to large; Ptarmigans Pop Up Park sits in front of the Main Base Lodge for smaller features when conditions allow; Family Cross is a cross-style course for everyone. No feature counts, no lighting and no rebuild schedule are published, and there is no pipe.
parks.reputation: Better than Attitash's family-mountain reputation implies. The resort describes freestyle as a vital part of its culture and keeps a dedicated park crew, and three parks on 311 acres is a real commitment for a mountain this size - Mount Sunapee, its larger Vail sibling, publishes a park count and not one park name. That said, nothing here competes with Carinthia at Mount Snow, and a serious park rider in New Hampshire is more likely to be at Loon or Waterville.
